subject: Inglês
title: Semantics

scope.covers: Semantics of English: lexical and sentence meaning, reference and sense, semantic relations, ambiguity, compositionality, truth conditions, entailment, contradiction, presupposition, quantification, thematic roles, and the distinction between semantic meaning and pragmatic inference, with concrete English examples.
scope.excludes: Phonetics, phonology, syntax as a full subject, discourse analysis, literary interpretation, and detailed formal logic beyond what is needed to explain English meaning.

chapters.title: 1. Words, concepts, sense and reference
chapters.markdown:
### O problema que este assunto resolve

Semantics studies linguistic meaning. It asks what a word or sentence conventionally contributes and how those contributions combine. It differs from syntax, which studies how words are arranged, and from phonology, which studies sound patterns. The English sentences *The cat chased the rat* and *The rat chased the cat* contain the same words but assign different participants to the action because their structure differs.

> **Siglas e termos deste capítulo**
> - **Lexical meaning**: meaning associated with a word or vocabulary item.
> - **Sense**: a concept or mode of presentation associated with an expression.
> - **Reference**: the person, object, place, or situation an expression picks out in context.
> - **Lexeme**: an abstract vocabulary item, including its inflected forms.

A proper name such as *London* can refer to a particular city. A description such as *the capital of the United Kingdom* can refer to the same city while presenting it differently. Expressions can therefore share a referent without having identical senses. Conversely, the same expression may refer to different things in different contexts: *I*, *here*, and *today* depend on who speaks, where, and when.

Words also form semantic relations. *Poodle* is a hyponym of *dog*: every poodle is a dog, but not every dog is a poodle. *Dog* is the superordinate term, or hypernym. *Rose* and *tulip* are co-hyponyms under *flower*. Near-synonyms such as *begin* and *start* have similar meanings but may differ in register or collocation: *begin a journey* and *start a journey* are both natural, while some fixed expressions prefer one form.

Antonyms are not all alike. *Hot/cold* are gradable opposites: something can be warm or cool between the endpoints. *Alive/dead* are commonly treated as complementary opposites in ordinary contexts. *Buy/sell* describe the same transaction from converse perspectives: if Dana buys a book from Lee, Lee sells the book to Dana. *Bank* (financial institution / side of a river) illustrates homonymy when unrelated meanings share a form; *head* (body part / leader / top) illustrates related senses, or polysemy. Context normally selects the intended reading.

### How cai na prova

- Check the direction of inclusion: every poodle is a dog, not every dog a poodle.
- Ask whether two expressions pick out the same thing (reference) or present it in the same way (sense).
- Distinguish gradable opposites, complementary opposites, and converse pairs.
- Treat a context-dependent word like *I* as an expression whose referent changes with the speaker, not as a word with no meaning.

chapters.title: 2. Sentence meaning, structure and truth conditions
chapters.markdown:
### O problema que este assunto resolve

A speaker can understand a sentence without knowing whether it is true in the actual world. Knowing the meaning includes knowing what would have to be the case for it to be true: its **truth conditions**. *The door is open* is true in a situation in which the relevant door is open and false in one in which it is closed. Its truth value may change as the situation changes, while its conventional meaning remains stable.

> **Siglas e termos deste capítulo**
> - **Proposition**: the content expressed by a declarative sentence in a context, capable of being true or false.
> - **Truth conditions**: the circumstances under which a proposition is true.
> - **Compositionality**: sentence meaning is computed from the meanings of its parts and how they are combined.
> - **Predicate**: an expression that attributes a property or relation, such as *sleep* or *admire*.

Compositionality explains how speakers understand novel sentences. In *Maya opened the small box*, the words contribute their meanings, while syntax identifies *Maya* as the opener, *the small box* as what was opened, and *small* as a modifier of *box*. Reordering the noun phrases changes who did what: *The dog bit the postman* differs from *The postman bit the dog*.

In a basic model, an intransitive predicate such as *sleep* is true of individuals who sleep. An adjective such as *red* applies to things with that property. A transitive verb such as *admire* relates two participants: in *Nina admires Omar*, Nina is the admirer and Omar is the person admired. The same participants reversed do not generally make the same sentence true.

Logical words also contribute predictable meaning. In ordinary truth-functional interpretation, *and* requires both conjuncts to be true; *or* is inclusive unless context suggests otherwise, so it is true if either or both disjuncts are true. *Not P* is true when P is false. The basic material conditional *if P, Q* is false only when P is true and Q is false, though natural-language conditionals often convey additional contextual or causal expectations.

### Como cai na prova

- A sentence may be meaningful but false; meaning is not the same as actual truth.
- When participants change places around a transitive verb, check the changed relation.
- In logic questions, distinguish the truth-conditional contribution of *or* from an exclusivity inference supplied by context.
- Do not confuse the compositional rule with a word-by-word list: syntactic structure matters.

chapters.title: 3. Semantic relations between sentences
chapters.markdown:
### O problema que este assunto resolve

Sentence relations let us test what follows from what. If one sentence entails another, the second must be true whenever the first is true, under the same interpretation and relevant context. *Milo is a poodle* entails *Milo is a dog*. It does not entail *Milo is friendly*: that could be false while the first sentence is true.

> **Siglas e termos deste capítulo**
> - **Entailment**: a truth-preserving consequence from one proposition to another.
> - **Contradiction**: propositions that cannot both be true in the same circumstances.
> - **Paraphrase**: expressions with substantially equivalent truth conditions in a stated context.
> - **Implicature**: a context-based inference that can often be cancelled without contradiction.

Two propositions contradict when they cannot both be true in the same circumstances. *The light is on* and *The light is not on* contradict, assuming the same light, time, and sense of *on*. A pair can be compatible without one entailing the other: *Rae owns a bicycle* and *Rae owns a helmet* could both be true, but neither follows from the other.

Paraphrase is stronger than topical similarity. *The committee approved the plan* and *The plan was approved by the committee* can describe the same event and have similar truth conditions. Their information structure differs, but the core participants and event remain. By contrast, *The committee considered the plan* does not entail approval.

Entailment is not the same as conversational implicature. *Some of the guests arrived* semantically permits all of them to have arrived. A listener may infer “not all” because a more informative alternative (*all*) was available, but that inference can be cancelled: *Some, in fact all, arrived.* The cancellation sounds coherent, which shows that “not all” is usually an implicature rather than an entailment of *some*.

### Como cai na prova

- Test entailment by imagining the first statement true and the alleged consequence false. If that situation is possible, entailment fails.
- Keep referents, time, and word senses constant when judging contradiction.
- Try cancelling a supposed inference: a natural cancellation is evidence that it is pragmatic rather than truth-conditional.
- A passive paraphrase may preserve core truth conditions while changing which participant is foregrounded.

chapters.title: 4. Presupposition, reference and quantification
chapters.markdown:
### O problema que este assunto resolve

Some expressions carry background assumptions that are not the main assertion. In *Jordan stopped smoking*, the verb *stopped* normally presupposes that Jordan used to smoke; the sentence asserts that Jordan no longer does. The background assumption commonly survives negation and questions: *Jordan did not stop smoking* and *Did Jordan stop smoking?* still normally take for granted that Jordan smoked before.

> **Siglas e termos deste capítulo**
> - **Presupposition**: background content treated as already accepted or suitable for the conversation.
> - **Trigger**: a word or construction that tends to introduce a presupposition.
> - **Definite description**: a phrase such as *the red car*, often used for a contextually identifiable individual.
> - **Quantifier**: an expression such as *every*, *some*, or *no* that specifies quantity or distribution.

Common English triggers include *again* (*Lee called again* suggests Lee called before), *too* (*Ava came too* suggests someone relevant also came), *know* (*Sam knows that the gate is locked* presents the gate's being locked as backgrounded), and definite descriptions (*the manager* normally assumes a contextually identifiable manager). These assumptions can be challenged when they are false or disputed.

Quantifiers have different force. *Every student passed* requires each individual in the relevant student group to have passed. *Some students passed* requires at least one, but does not semantically rule out all. *No student passed* excludes any student passing. The relevant domain is often restricted by context: *Everyone is ready* usually means everyone in the relevant group, not every person in the world.

Pronouns and demonstratives depend on context or discourse. In *I left my keys here yesterday*, the speaker fixes *I*, the location of *here*, and the date of *yesterday*. *This* and *that* may point to visible objects or to material in the conversation. These are deictic uses. An antecedent can also identify a pronoun: in *Priya found a wallet and returned it*, *it* refers back to *a wallet*.

### Como cai na prova

- For a presupposition, inspect both the positive sentence and its negation or question.
- *Some* does not mean “some but not all” as a strict semantic entailment.
- Quantifier scope is restricted by the stated or understood domain.
- Identify whether a pronoun is anchored to the speech situation or to an earlier noun phrase.

chapters.title: 5. Ambiguity, roles and semantics in context
chapters.markdown:
### O problema que este assunto resolve

A sentence can have more than one interpretation because a word has multiple senses or because its structure allows more than one grouping. *I saw her duck* can mean that I saw her lower her head, or that I saw a duck belonging to her. This is ambiguity, not necessarily vagueness. *Tall* is vague because borderline cases exist; it does not usually alternate between two unrelated readings.

> **Siglas e termos deste capítulo**
> - **Lexical ambiguity**: multiple senses associated with one word form.
> - **Structural ambiguity**: more than one syntactic grouping and corresponding interpretation.
> - **Thematic role**: a participant's semantic relation to an event, such as agent, patient, experiencer, or instrument.
> - **Pragmatics**: interpretation shaped by context, speaker goals, and conversational expectations.

Thematic roles describe meaning rather than grammatical labels. In *The key opened the door*, *the key* is an instrument or cause, not an intentional agent. In *Lena broke the glass*, Lena is the agent and the glass is the affected patient or theme. In *Owen fears storms*, Owen is an experiencer. A grammatical subject can therefore have different semantic roles in different sentences.

Semantics and pragmatics interact but are not identical. *Can you pass the salt?* literally asks about ability, but in an ordinary meal it functions as a request. *It is cold here* may be a report about temperature or an indirect request to close a window. The conventional sentence meaning constrains interpretation; the situation and shared assumptions help identify the speaker's intended action.

Context can also resolve reference and ambiguity without changing the lexical entry. In *Put it there*, the object and location must be supplied by the situation. In *The old men and women sat down*, grouping may mean old men plus women of any age, or old men and old women. Punctuation or a clearer rewrite can remove the ambiguity.

### Como cai na prova

- Give two readings to show ambiguity; give a scale or borderline case to show vagueness.
- Determine thematic roles from the event relation, not from subject/object position alone.
- Separate what a sentence conventionally says from what a speaker indirectly communicates.
- Use nearby words, discourse, and physical setting to resolve context-sensitive expressions.

summary: Semantics is the study of linguistic meaning. English words have lexical meanings and enter relations such as synonymy, hyponymy, antonymy, homonymy, and polysemy. Sense is a way of presenting meaning; reference is what an expression picks out in context. Sentence interpretation is compositional: lexical meanings combine according to syntactic structure and yield truth conditions. Entailment is a truth-preserving consequence; contradiction excludes joint truth; conversational implicatures are context-based and often cancellable. Presupposition is backgrounded content, often triggered by words such as stop, again, too, know, and definite descriptions. Quantifiers include every, some, and no, with domains restricted by context. Pronouns and demonstratives depend on discourse or the speech situation. Ambiguity may be lexical or structural; vagueness has borderline cases. Thematic roles identify participants as agents, patients, experiencers, or instruments. Pragmatics explains how context and speaker intentions supplement conventional sentence meaning.

flashcards.back: Linguistic meaning in words, phrases, and sentences, including how meanings combine and relate to situations.

flashcards.front: How do semantics and syntax differ?
flashcards.back: Semantics studies meaning; syntax studies how words and phrases are structured and combined.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between sense and reference?
flashcards.back: Sense is a way of presenting an expression's meaning; reference is the entity it picks out in a context.
The meaning of a complex expression depends on its parts and the way they are syntactically combined.
The circumstances that must hold for a proposition to be true.
A relation in which the truth of one proposition guarantees the truth of another under the same interpretation.

flashcards.front: Does 'some students passed' entail that not all passed?
flashcards.back: No. Some requires at least one; 'not all' is often a cancellable conversational inference.
A pair of propositions that cannot both be true in the same circumstances and interpretation.
A more specific term included under a broader term; every poodle is a dog, so poodle is a hyponym of dog.
A broader category term; dog is a hypernym of poodle.

flashcards.front: How do homonymy and polysemy differ?
flashcards.back: Homonymy involves a shared form with unrelated meanings; polysemy involves related senses of one form.
A pair describing one relation from opposite participant perspectives, as buy and sell.
Background content treated as accepted or appropriate for the utterance, rather than its main assertion.

flashcards.front: What does 'stop' presuppose in 'Mia stopped running'?
flashcards.back: That Mia had been running before the stopping point.
That the relevant event or state occurred before.
A lexical item or grammatical construction associated with a presupposition.

flashcards.front: What does 'every' mean in a quantified sentence?
flashcards.back: It applies the predicate to each member of the contextually relevant domain.
That zero individuals in the relevant student group passed.

flashcards.front: What are deixis and a deictic expression?
flashcards.back: Deixis anchors interpretation to the speech situation; I, here, and today are deictic expressions.
Two or more interpretations produced by different possible groupings of the same words.

flashcards.front: How does vagueness differ from ambiguity?
flashcards.back: Vagueness has borderline cases on a scale; ambiguity has distinct readings.
The participant that intentionally or causally initiates an event, depending on the verb and context.
The participant affected or changed by an event.
The participant who feels, perceives, or experiences a mental state, as Owen in 'Owen fears storms'.
A context-supported inference beyond literal truth conditions, often cancellable without contradiction.

tips: To test entailment, imagine the first sentence true and the alleged consequence false; if that is possible, entailment fails.
For word relations, check direction: every poodle is a dog, but not every dog is a poodle.
When evaluating truth, hold the relevant person, time, place, and word sense constant.
To identify a presupposition, check whether the background assumption survives negation or a question.
Separate semantic content from a likely conversational inference by testing whether the inference can be cancelled.
Assign thematic roles from the event described; a subject is not automatically an agent.
traps: Treating the inference 'some but not all' as part of the strict meaning of some; all may still be true.
Reversing hyponymy: poodle is more specific than dog, while dog is the hypernym.
Calling every change in truth value a change in sentence meaning; situations can change while truth conditions stay stable.
Assuming negation removes a presupposition; 'Jordan did not stop smoking' still normally assumes prior smoking.
Equating ambiguity with vagueness; ambiguity has separate readings, while vagueness has a fuzzy boundary.
Equating grammatical subject with agent; an instrument can be a subject, as in 'The key opened the door'.

activeRecall.question: Explain the difference between sense and reference using two English expressions for one city.
activeRecall.answer: London and the capital of the United Kingdom can refer to the same city while presenting it through different senses: a name versus a descriptive phrase.

activeRecall.question: Why do the sentences 'The cat chased the rat' and 'The rat chased the cat' differ in meaning?
activeRecall.answer: Their syntax assigns the cat and rat to different participant positions, changing who performs the chasing and who is chased.

activeRecall.question: Give an entailment and explain why it holds.
activeRecall.answer: Milo is a poodle entails Milo is a dog because being a poodle necessarily places Milo in the dog category.

activeRecall.question: Why is 'not all' usually not entailed by 'some'?
activeRecall.answer: Some requires at least one but allows all. A speaker can say 'Some arrived—in fact, all of them did' without contradiction.

activeRecall.question: Identify the assertion and presupposition in 'Ava called again'.
activeRecall.answer: The assertion is that Ava called; again backgrounds that a relevant earlier call occurred.

activeRecall.question: How can the context determine the referent of I, here, and today?
activeRecall.answer: The speaker determines I, the location of the utterance determines here, and its date determines today.

activeRecall.question: Distinguish lexical ambiguity from structural ambiguity.
activeRecall.answer: Lexical ambiguity arises from multiple senses of a word; structural ambiguity arises from multiple phrase groupings, as in 'I saw her duck'.

activeRecall.question: Why is the subject of 'The key opened the door' not necessarily an agent?
activeRecall.answer: The key is an instrument or cause in the event and does not intentionally perform the action; grammatical subject position does not determine thematic role.

errorConcepts.title: Word relations reversed
errorConcepts.summary: A hyponym is the narrower term and a hypernym the broader one; antonyms can be gradable, complementary, or converse.

errorConcepts.title: Truth conditions confused with actual truth
errorConcepts.summary: Meaning specifies circumstances for truth; a meaningful sentence can be false, and the same sentence may change truth value across situations.

errorConcepts.title: Entailment confused with implicature
errorConcepts.summary: Entailment cannot be cancelled while retaining the premise; many conversational inferences, including not all from some, can be cancelled.

errorConcepts.title: Presupposition missed under negation
errorConcepts.summary: Triggers such as stop, again, too, and definite descriptions commonly maintain background assumptions in questions and negative clauses.

errorConcepts.title: Grammar labels mistaken for semantic roles
errorConcepts.summary: Subject and object are grammatical relations; agent, patient, experiencer, and instrument are semantic roles and need not map one-to-one.

questions.statement: What does semantics primarily investigate in the study of English?

options.text: The sound waves and physical production of each English speech sound.
The meanings of words and sentences and how those meanings relate.
The spelling conventions that distinguish British and American English.
The historical sequence in which English borrowed words from French.
The social rules that govern turn-taking in every conversation.

questions.explanation: Semantics concerns linguistic meaning at word and sentence level and the relations among meanings. Speech sounds belong mainly to phonetics and phonology; spelling history, etymology, and conversational turn-taking are distinct topics.

questions.statement: Which pair illustrates a difference between sense and reference?

options.text: The expressions have different sounds and must name different objects.
The phrases have the same spelling and therefore the same interpretation.
The words are synonyms because both refer to a city in England.
The name London and the description the capital of the UK can pick out one city in different ways.
The description has no sense because it can refer to more than one place.

questions.explanation: Reference is the entity picked out; sense is the way an expression presents it. A name and a definite description can refer to London while having different senses. Different sounds do not force distinct referents, and descriptions remain meaningful.

questions.statement: In the pair poodle and dog, which statement correctly describes the lexical relation?

options.text: Dog is a hyponym of poodle because it names the narrower class.
Poodle and dog are unrelated because one is a breed and one is an animal.
Poodle is a hyponym of dog, and dog is its hypernym.
Poodle and dog are converse terms for the same animal relation.
Poodle is a synonym of dog because every poodle is also a dog.

questions.explanation: A hyponym is more specific: every poodle is a dog. The broader category is the hypernym. Inclusion does not make the terms synonyms, since many dogs are not poodles, and the relation is not converse.

questions.statement: Which example most clearly shows a converse relation?

options.text: Ava buys a book from Ben; Ben sells that book to Ava.
A red car is a car, and a blue car is also a car.
A kettle is hot, while the same kettle can later become cold.
A rose is a flower, and a tulip is a kind of flower.
A bank holds deposits, while a river bank borders flowing water.

questions.explanation: Buy and sell describe the same transaction from the buyer's and seller's perspectives. The other pairs illustrate category inclusion, gradable opposition, co-hyponymy, and unrelated homonymous senses.

questions.statement: Which description best distinguishes homonymy from polysemy?

options.text: Homonyms are always pronounced alike, while polysemous words are always spelled alike.
Polysemy occurs only between words from different languages, unlike homonymy.
Homonymy is a relation between opposites, while polysemy is a relation between synonyms.
Homonymy involves unrelated meanings sharing a form; polysemy involves related senses.
Homonymy has one meaning, whereas polysemy has no interpretable meaning.

questions.explanation: The distinction concerns whether the readings are unrelated or connected senses of a lexical item. English bank for a financial institution and river edge is a familiar homonymy example; head has related uses for body part, leader, and top.

questions.statement: The opposite pair hot and cold differs from alive and dead because hot and cold are commonly treated as what kind of opposites?

options.text: Converses, since one participant can hot another participant.
Gradable antonyms, since intermediate states such as warm are possible.
Hyponyms, since cold is a narrower kind of hot condition.
Homonyms, since both words refer to the same temperature.
Complementaries, since no intermediate temperature can be described.

questions.explanation: Hot and cold lie on a scale with possible intermediate descriptions such as warm or cool. Alive and dead are more commonly treated as complementary opposites in ordinary contexts, though real-world classification can introduce edge cases.

questions.statement: What makes I, here, and today context-dependent expressions?

options.text: Each expression changes its grammatical category in every sentence.
Their meaning is determined by the nearest adjective in the clause.
They always refer to the same speaker, location, and calendar date.
They lack conventional meaning and can only be interpreted by guessing.
Their referents depend on the speaker and circumstances of utterance.

questions.explanation: These deictic expressions are anchored to the speech situation: I to the speaker, here to the relevant location, and today to the utterance date. Their referents can change between utterances while the expressions retain their conventional meaning.

questions.statement: A learner understands a sentence that has never been heard before by combining known word meanings with its structure. Which principle does this illustrate?

options.text: Presupposition, because every new sentence assumes a shared history.
Deixis, because novel sentences always point at visible objects.
Compositionality, because meanings combine according to syntactic structure.
Homonymy, because each new sentence repeats a word form.
Contradiction, because new combinations negate familiar meanings.

questions.explanation: Compositionality explains how finite lexical and grammatical resources support interpretation of novel sentences. Presupposition and deixis can affect particular utterances, but they do not explain this general productivity.
questions.section: 2. Sentence meaning, structure and truth conditions

questions.statement: If The door is open is true exactly in situations where the relevant door is open, what has been specified?

options.text: The truth conditions of the sentence in the relevant context.
The historical origin of the word door in English.
The presupposition that every door is made of wood.
The conversational implicature that someone entered the room.
The grammatical role of open as the sentence subject.

questions.explanation: Truth conditions characterize the circumstances in which a proposition is true. The sentence does not itself assert that anyone entered, that all doors are wooden, or that the adjective is the subject.
questions.section: 2. Sentence meaning, structure and truth conditions

questions.statement: How does changing The dog bit the postman to The postman bit the dog affect the interpretation?

options.text: It preserves the event because English word order has no semantic effect.
It changes only politeness, leaving the participants' roles fixed.
It adds a presupposition that both participants were injured.
It changes which participant is represented as biting and which is bitten.
It makes the second sentence a question about the same event.

questions.explanation: English syntax assigns the subject and object different semantic relations to the transitive verb. Reversing the noun phrases changes the represented event; it does not merely alter style or sentence type.
questions.section: 2. Sentence meaning, structure and truth conditions

questions.statement: Under the ordinary inclusive truth-conditional interpretation of or, when is P or Q true?

options.text: Only when P and Q are both true at the same moment.
When at least one of P and Q is true, including when both are true.
Only when exactly one of P and Q is true and the other is false.
Whenever P is false, regardless of the truth of Q.
Only when the speaker explicitly rejects both alternatives.

questions.explanation: Inclusive disjunction is true if P, Q, or both are true. Context can create an exclusive inference, but that is not the basic truth-conditional meaning of or.
questions.section: 2. Sentence meaning, structure and truth conditions

questions.statement: If Rae owns a bicycle and Rae owns a helmet can both be true, but neither statement guarantees the other, what relation do they have?

options.text: They are contradictions because one excludes the other.
They stand in entailment because bicycle ownership entails a helmet.
They are equivalent paraphrases with matching truth conditions.
They are converse descriptions of one purchase transaction.
They are compatible propositions with no entailment between them.

questions.explanation: The propositions can both hold, so they are not contradictory. Neither follows necessarily from the other: owning a bicycle does not guarantee owning a helmet, and owning a helmet does not guarantee a bicycle.

questions.statement: Which sentence pair is a clear contradiction when it concerns the same light at the same time?

options.text: The light is on; the bulb is new.
The light is bright; the light is visible.
The light is on; the light is not on.
The light is on; the room is warm.
The light is bright; its cover is made of glass.

questions.explanation: A proposition and its negation cannot both be true under the same interpretation and circumstances. The other pairs can consistently be true together.

questions.statement: If Milo is a poodle is true, which statement must also be true because of lexical category inclusion?

options.text: Milo is friendly to every visitor who approaches him.
Milo is the oldest dog living in his neighborhood.
Milo has lived with the same family since birth.
Milo is a dog.
Milo has won a competition for working dogs.

questions.explanation: Poodle is a hyponym of dog, so membership in the narrower class entails membership in the broader class. Friendliness, age, ownership history, and competition results are not entailed by being a poodle.

questions.statement: Which continuation cancels the usual inference from Some of the guests arrived without contradiction?

options.text: Some of the guests arrived—in fact, all of them arrived.
Some of the guests arrived, so not one guest arrived.
Some of the guests arrived, although none of the guests arrived.
Some of the guests arrived, which proves that every guest stayed away.
Some of the guests arrived, and therefore no guest came to the party.

questions.explanation: Some is true when at least one relevant guest arrived, including the case where all did. The inference that not all arrived is typically conversational and can be explicitly cancelled; the other continuations conflict with the first clause.

questions.statement: The committee approved the plan and The plan was approved by the committee describe the same approval event. What relation is most plausible?

options.text: They are contradictory because one is active and the other is passive.
They can be paraphrases with similar truth conditions and different focus.
They have no shared meaning because passive clauses omit all participants.
The passive sentence entails that the committee rejected the plan.
The active sentence presupposes that the plan was never discussed.

questions.explanation: The active and passive versions assign the same approval relation to the committee and plan while foregrounding different participants. A passive construction may omit an agent, but here it is overtly expressed in the by-phrase.

questions.statement: What does Jordan stopped smoking normally presuppose?

options.text: Jordan has never smoked at any time in the past.
Jordan will certainly begin smoking again tomorrow.
Jordan persuaded another person to stop smoking.
Jordan used to smoke before the relevant stopping point.
Jordan dislikes every person who continues smoking.

questions.explanation: Stop typically backgrounds that the activity held before it ceased. The sentence asserts cessation; it does not say Jordan will resume, influenced anyone else, or has a particular attitude toward smokers.

questions.statement: Which background assumption normally remains in Did Lee call again?

options.text: Lee called before the relevant possible call.
Lee called every person in the speaker's contact list.
Lee has never used a telephone before today.
The speaker already knows Lee will call again tomorrow.
The question itself asserts that Lee's new call occurred.

questions.explanation: Again commonly presupposes an earlier occurrence of the relevant event. The question asks whether another call occurred and does not assert that the new call happened or predict future calls.

questions.statement: What does Some students passed assert at minimum, without extra contextual inference?

options.text: Every student in every school passed the relevant exam.
Exactly half of the students passed, with no more than that.
At least one student in the relevant group passed.
No student in the relevant class achieved a passing score.
The students passed only after the speaker asked them to leave.

questions.explanation: Some gives existential quantity: there is at least one relevant student who passed. It does not specify an exact proportion or exclude the possibility that all students passed.

questions.statement: In a classroom context, Everyone is ready normally quantifies over which group?

options.text: Every human being who has ever lived on Earth.
Every person relevant in the classroom context, unless expanded.
Only the teacher, because everyone is a singular noun.
Only people who are physically outside the classroom.
An unrestricted set that cannot be narrowed by context.

questions.explanation: Natural-language quantifiers commonly have contextually restricted domains. In a classroom, everyone normally means the relevant classroom group, not the entire population of the world.

questions.statement: In Sam did not stop smoking, what remains a normal background assumption despite negation?

options.text: Sam has never smoked and has no familiarity with tobacco.
Sam stopped smoking, although the sentence denies it.
Sam has decided to start smoking for the first time.
Sam's neighbors all smoke during the day.
Sam used to smoke, though the sentence denies that stopping occurred.

questions.explanation: Negation targets the asserted stopping event, while stop normally preserves the presupposition that the activity occurred earlier. Thus the sentence denies cessation while backgrounding prior smoking.

questions.statement: In Priya found a wallet and returned it, what most naturally supplies the reference of it?

options.text: The speaker's location at the time of the utterance.
The present calendar date shared by the listeners.
The person who is listening to Priya's story.
The previously introduced noun phrase a wallet.
An object that cannot be recovered from the sentence or context.

questions.explanation: The pronoun it is anaphoric: the earlier noun phrase a wallet supplies its discourse antecedent. It is not deictic in this example because interpretation does not require pointing to a visible object.

questions.statement: How does lexical ambiguity differ from vagueness?

options.text: Lexical ambiguity has distinct readings; vagueness has borderline cases on a scale.
Lexical ambiguity occurs only in writing, while vagueness occurs only in speech.
Vagueness gives a word unrelated dictionary entries, but ambiguity gives a precise boundary.
Both terms mean that a sentence has no possible interpretation.
Ambiguity is caused by context, while vagueness is caused only by spelling.

questions.explanation: Ambiguity involves multiple readings, whether lexical or structural. A vague expression such as tall has cases near the boundary where its application is not sharp, rather than two unrelated readings.
questions.section: 5. Ambiguity, roles and semantics in context

questions.statement: What are the two plausible readings of I saw her duck?

options.text: I saw her, and I saw a duck that belonged to an unrelated person.
I heard her speak, or I saw her write a note about a bird.
I saw her lower her head, or I saw a duck belonging to her.
I watched her swim, or she watched me feed a duck.
I saw a duck, and her name was also Duck in the same sentence.

questions.explanation: Duck can be a noun naming a bird or a verb meaning lower the head/body, producing lexical ambiguity and different structures. The supplied sentence supports both readings without extra words.
questions.section: 5. Ambiguity, roles and semantics in context

questions.statement: In Lena broke the glass, which participant is most clearly the affected patient or theme?

options.text: Lena, because the grammatical subject is always the affected participant.
The glass, because it is the participant affected by the breaking event.
The verb broke, because verbs receive the patient role in clauses.
The speaker, because every assertion assigns the speaker an event role.
Neither noun phrase, because English clauses do not express participants.

questions.explanation: The glass undergoes the change associated with breaking, so it is the affected patient or theme. Lena is the agent in the ordinary reading; semantic roles describe participants, not grammatical categories alone.
questions.section: 5. Ambiguity, roles and semantics in context

questions.statement: In The key opened the door, what role does the key most naturally play?

options.text: The experiencer who felt surprise when the door moved.
The patient that changed from a key into an open door.
The person who intentionally chose to unlock the door.
The instrument or cause by which the door was opened.
The location where the opening event happened.

questions.explanation: The key is an instrument or cause enabling the opening. Although it is the grammatical subject, an inanimate key is not normally an intentional agent; the door is the affected participant.
questions.section: 5. Ambiguity, roles and semantics in context

questions.statement: Why can Can you pass the salt? function as a request at dinner even though its literal form asks about ability?

options.text: Because pass has no lexical meaning when it occurs in a question.
Because every English question conventionally orders the listener to act.
Because the sentence semantically entails that the salt has been passed.
Because ability questions cannot receive a truth value in any situation.
Because context and cooperative inference support an indirect request reading.

questions.explanation: The literal question concerns the listener's ability, while the dinner setting makes a polite request a likely intended act. This is pragmatic interpretation built on, rather than erasing, sentence meaning.
questions.section: 5. Ambiguity, roles and semantics in context

questions.statement: A speaker says It is cold here while standing beside an open window. Which interpretation best separates semantics from pragmatics?

options.text: The words have no conventional content because the sentence is indirect.
The sentence conventionally describes temperature, and context may suggest closing the window.
The sentence entails that the listener must close the window immediately.
The sentence presupposes that the window was broken by the listener.
Pragmatics determines the dictionary meaning of cold in every use.

questions.explanation: The conventional sentence content concerns the temperature at the contextually relevant place. The open window and conversational situation can support an indirect request, but that request is not entailed by the sentence.
questions.section: 5. Ambiguity, roles and semantics in context

questions.statement: The statement The door is open can be true in one situation and false in another while keeping its ordinary meaning. Is this correct?

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Certo. Its truth value depends on the state of the relevant door at the evaluation time. The truth conditions remain the same even as the world changes and makes the sentence true or false.
questions.section: 2. Sentence meaning, structure and truth conditions

questions.statement: Compositionality says that the interpretation of a complex English expression depends on its parts and the way they are syntactically combined.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Certo. The principle accounts for how speakers interpret new combinations from familiar lexical meanings and grammatical structure, rather than memorizing every sentence as a whole.
questions.section: 2. Sentence meaning, structure and truth conditions

questions.statement: Because poodle is a hyponym of dog, the statement Milo is a dog entails Milo is a poodle.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Errado. The inclusion goes from the narrower class to the broader one: being a poodle entails being a dog. A dog need not be a poodle, so the proposed inference reverses the direction.

questions.statement: In the sentence Some students passed, the word some semantically excludes the possibility that every student passed.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Errado. Some requires at least one member of the relevant group, but all may have passed. The suggestion that not all passed is a common cancellable conversational implicature, not a strict entailment.

questions.statement: The pair buy and sell can describe the same transaction from the buyer's and seller's perspectives.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Certo. If Morgan buys a coat from Alex, Alex sells that coat to Morgan. The predicates are converses because they reverse which participant occupies each perspective in one relation.

questions.statement: Homonymy and polysemy both involve a word form with multiple readings, but polysemy relates those readings as senses of one lexical item.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Certo. Polysemy concerns related senses, such as head of a body and head of an organization. Homonymy is used for unrelated meanings sharing a form, as with financial bank and river bank.

questions.statement: The terms hot and cold are gradable opposites because speakers can use intermediate descriptions such as warm and cool.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Certo. Gradable antonyms lie on a scale and allow intermediate values. This contrasts with pairs commonly treated as complementary, such as alive and dead in ordinary contexts.

questions.statement: A speaker may understand the truth conditions of a sentence even when the speaker does not know whether the sentence is true in the actual situation.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Certo. Knowing the meaning involves knowing what would make the sentence true, not necessarily knowing whether those conditions obtain now. A person can understand The door is open without seeing the door.
questions.section: 2. Sentence meaning, structure and truth conditions

questions.statement: The statement The light is on and The light is not on can both be true at the same time if both refer to the same light and use the same sense of on.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Errado. A proposition and its negation contradict under a fixed interpretation and time. Changing the time or referent could remove the conflict, but the statement specifies the same light and moment.

questions.statement: If a sentence entails another, it is possible for the first to be true while the second is false under the same interpretation.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Errado. Entailment means that whenever the first proposition is true, the second must also be true under the same interpretation. A possible counterexample situation shows that entailment does not hold.

questions.statement: The verbs stop and again can trigger background assumptions about an earlier activity or event.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Certo. Stop commonly presupposes that an activity held before cessation, while again commonly presupposes a prior occurrence. These are examples of lexical presupposition triggers.

questions.statement: In ordinary use, the presupposition of Jordan stopped smoking commonly remains backgrounded in the negative sentence Jordan did not stop smoking.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Certo. Negation denies the asserted stopping, but the trigger stop still commonly backgrounds that Jordan smoked before. This persistence under negation is a useful diagnostic for presupposition.

questions.statement: In a classroom, Everyone is ready normally means every person in the world is ready, since context cannot limit quantifier domains.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Errado. Context commonly restricts the relevant domain of a quantifier. In a classroom, everyone normally concerns the people relevant to that setting, not every person on Earth.

questions.statement: The expression here can refer to different locations in two utterances because it is anchored to the utterance context.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Certo. Here is deictic: the location relevant to the speaker's utterance fixes its reference. Its referent can vary between contexts even though its conventional meaning remains stable.

questions.statement: The sentence I saw her duck has a single reading because duck can only be a noun in English.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Errado. Duck can be a noun for a bird or a verb meaning lower the head or body. The sentence therefore permits distinct readings supported by different lexical and structural analyses.
questions.section: 5. Ambiguity, roles and semantics in context

questions.statement: A grammatical subject is always an intentional agent, so the key in The key opened the door must have acted deliberately.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Errado. The key is the grammatical subject but normally functions as an instrument or cause, not an intentional agent. Semantic roles are not determined solely by subject position.
questions.section: 5. Ambiguity, roles and semantics in context

questions.statement: Can you pass the salt? can be a polite request in a meal context even though it literally asks about ability.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Certo. The conventional interrogative concerns ability, while the setting and cooperative expectations support an indirect request. The intended action is pragmatic enrichment, not literal entailment.
questions.section: 5. Ambiguity, roles and semantics in context

questions.statement: An implicature is necessarily part of a sentence's truth conditions and cannot be cancelled by a follow-up clause.

options.text: Certo
Errado

questions.explanation: Errado. Conversational implicatures are inferred from context and expectations, and many can be cancelled coherently. The follow-up Some arrived—in fact, all of them did cancels the usual not-all inference.
